title: Recon
tagline: Verifies what AI agents claim vs. what they actually did — and what their mandate allowed.
description:
RECON — Mandate Reconciliation for AI Agents                                                                          
                                                                                                                        
  Everyone is putting leashes on AI agents (spending caps, allowlists, session keys), but almost nobody verifies that   
  the leash actually holds. RECON is a reconciliation layer that answers that question, rather than being yet another   
  agent wallet.   
                                                                                                                        
  RECON reconciles three views of the same agent activity and turns any disagreement into independently re-verifiable   
  evidence:
                                                                                                                        
  - Claimed — what the agent says it did (query, payment, action), recorded as HCS messages with canonical hashes.      
  - Actual — what really happened on-chain, read from PolicyVault execution events and Hedera transactions.
  - Allowed — the mandate that was in effect at the moment of execution: budget cap, recipient allowlist, and deadline. 
                                                                                                                        
  Five deterministic rules (R1–R5) compare these three columns using one shared pure-TypeScript core: replaying a The   
  Graph query at a pinned deployment and final block, checking each executed action against the mandate valid at that   
  moment, verifying the claimed vs. actual executed set, validating HCS message ordering via a correlation state        
  machine, and matching payment claims against settlement receipts. Any inconsistency produces a MISMATCH with a
  deterministically derived evidenceHash; a down external service produces UNVERIFIABLE rather than being silently
  passed or failed.

  The agent runs on a restricted signer with no owner keys: it performs a live The Graph query, pays an x402-gated RECON
   verify-query API settled on Hedera testnet, selects a bounded action, executes through an on-chain PolicyVault (HBAR
  budget, allowlist, deadline, stake), and publishes its evidence to an HCS topic under a single correlation ID. A      
  public verifier — the same code the agent used — then replays everything from the Hedera mirror node, the Graph
  gateway, and payment receipts, and presents the Claimed / Actual / Allowed reconciliation in both a CLI and a React
  panel.

  Everything runs live against real services (real HCS messages, real vault transactions, real 402 payments) with no    
  mocks presented as evidence.
how_its_made:
RECON is TypeScript end to end, with one Solidity contract. The central design decision is that verification is a pure
   function: src/core holds the canonicalization, SHA-256 hashing (via @noble/hashes), correlation state machine, and   
  the R1–R5 reconciliation rules, and it never touches the network, environment variables, wallets, or the UI. Vendor
  behavior lives behind narrow adapters (src/adapters/thegraph, src/adapters/blocky402, src/adapters/hcs), and module   
  boundaries are enforced by ESLint import rules. The payoff: the agent and the public verifier literally run the same
  code, so CLI/Web parity is structural rather than something we tested into existence by hand.

  The on-chain side is a PolicyVault in Solidity 0.8.34, compiled with Hardhat 3 and driven through viem over the Hedera
   JSON-RPC relay. It separates owner / agent / verifier / operator roles, enforces an HBAR budget cap, recipient
  allowlist, and deadline before any transfer, isolates the operator's pre-funded stake from the vault principal, and   
  exposes a kill-switch that makes the next agent action revert with NotActive. Seven Solidity tests cover the mandate,
  roles, stake isolation, slashing, and the freeze.

  The application layer is strict TypeScript (Node ≥ 22.13) with zod validating every JSON boundary, a Vite 8 + React 19
   panel, and tsx-run scripts for probes and the live demo. The browser demo drives the whole loop through a single
  backend process — Graph query → x402 payment → DeepSeek rationale → vault execute → five HCS events → verify — so no  
  browser wallet is needed; slash and freeze are signed server-side from .env keys. The frontend implements no rules of
  its own; it renders the same LiveSnapshot the CLI verifier emits.

  Partner technologies, load-bearing:                                                                                   
  - Hedera — @hashgraph/sdk publishes the HCS evidence timeline under one correlation ID and reads it back from the
  mirror node; PolicyVault runs on testnet (chain 296).                                                                 
  - The Graph — a GraphQL query drives the agent's decision and is replayed at a pinned deployment + final block as R1
  evidence, using the same canonicalization and hash.                                                                   
  - x402 / Blocky402 — the verify-query API returns a 402 with exact/hedera:testnet requirements; the agent pays through
   the Blocky402 facilitator, which verifies and settles, and the response carries the on-chain settlement reference.   
  Payment success is deliberately independent of verification pass.                                                     
  - DeepSeek V4 Flash — picks between bounded EXECUTE_VAULT / STOP and writes a short rationale. The LLM never computes
  an amount, address, hash, or policy result; that's all deterministic code.                                            
                                                                                                                        
  Notable/hacky bits: the x402 payment header is generated in memory inside the same code path the web server uses, so
  the demo needs no separate api:start process or header round-trip. Hedera's public relay rejects wide eth_getLogs     
  spans, so verify:live starts its vault-log scan at the vault's deploy block (resolved from the mirror node). We hit
  the weibar-vs-tinybar trap — msg.value-style amounts are 18-decimal weibar while calldata amounts are 8-decimal       
  tinybar — and handle both explicitly. And when The Graph gateway prunes historical _meta.block.hash, we record it as
  null rather than fabricate it. Development was AI-assisted and disclosed; a human set scope and reviewed every change.
auto_summary: A TypeScript and Solidity system reconciles AI agent claims against Hedera activity, mandates, payments, and The Graph query results.
